extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly: scientists, educators, informed public (including farmers and practical men)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how scientific work and science writing should be presented to the public (clarity, breadth, pedagogy), together with prescriptive commentary on diagnosing/relieving economic overproduction in industry vs agriculture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate breadth beyond specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: The intense and prolonged concentration of thought upon special inquiries, when it becomes a habit, excludes that breadth of view which can only be attained by contemplating subjects in their wide relations; absorption in detail is inevitably unfavorable to the grasp of principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialists should keep up an interest in various subjects and the comprehensive results of research; avoid becoming 'mere specialists' who lose appreciation for generalization and the 'higher work of scientific generalization.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and respect the popularizer's role
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a prevalent illiberality among some scientific men who disparage those devoted to diffusing science; this contempt is often ungenerous and mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific men should not begrudge or disparage attempts to make science acceptable to the public; popular exposition is a legitimate and valuable activity that deserves sympathy and support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize exposition as a legitimate specialty
rubrics_metrics.description: The gift of interpreting the results of highly-special research for the benefit of those who are not prepared beforehand by special knowledge is by no means a common one — it is itself a specialty which very few have mastered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the ability to explain complex science clearly and lucidly as a recognized professional skill; avoid assuming that discovery and exposition are identical talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific societies should support education and curricula
rubrics_metrics.description: If our educational system fails to cultivate science, it is incumbent on influential scientific bodies to exert such an influence upon the schools as shall tend to secure the object; failing to do this, they are chargeable with culpable indifference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative scientific bodies should offer advice and respond to appeals from teachers and boards of education to organize science study — participation in shaping curricula is part of their responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate literary skill for attractive presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of vivid, effective presentation by language is difficult; many scientific professors fail in exposition before the public; if scientific men will not train themselves in the art of attractive popular exposition, let them not reproach others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists writing for broader audiences should seek literary training and strive to avoid bald, technical, involved, and repulsive styles; effective public teaching requires effort and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect facts to theory — theory matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts are of no value without theories. They are good for nothing until explained, or brought by reason into relation with other facts, so that some step is taken toward the establishment of a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value theoretical synthesis and the organization of observations into rational systems; do not magnify isolated facts while depreciating theorizing and generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrative cases and instructive notes in popular works
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Maudsley's book is enriched by instructive notes and quotations from authoritative writers, and by illustrative cases which add materially to the interest of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for popular or broad audiences, include concrete illustrative cases, instructive notes, and accessible quotations to engage readers and clarify abstract points (example: the locksmith/blind-boy anecdote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor technicality to audience — avoid unnecessary technicalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Prof. Riley, writing on the locust, avoids technicalities and writes in a style easily intelligible to the popular mind; the object is practical: to acquaint farmers with means of counteracting the plague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the target audience is practitioners or the general public, minimize specialist jargon and technical detail; emphasize practical, actionable guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish and structure works to serve differing audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Maudsley split a large work into two volumes (physiology of mind and mental pathology) so readers could choose the volume most relevant to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-faceted scholarly works, consider dividing material so that distinct audiences (general students vs medical professionals) can access the part most relevant to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit practical directions where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The lightning-protection treatise includes explicit directions for the protection of buildings of every description, ships, oil-tanks, steam-boilers, bridges, telegraph-poles, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical/practical publications intended to guide practitioners should include detailed, explicit instructions and applicability across common use-cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose root causes before prescribing remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: All efforts at relief from the dull times must lie in the same direction; the adjustment of the disturbed equilibrium in the productions will work itself out as soon as the true causes of the 'stagnation in trade' are clearly understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy recommendations and interventions should be based on a clear understanding of underlying causes rather than superficial remedies; diagnosis precedes effective cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural, non-legislative adjustments to economic imbalance
rubrics_metrics.description: No legislative or government interference is needed or desirable. The adjustment will work itself out as people change occupations; letting natural forces operate is the best remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When overproduction or sectoral glut is one-sided, encourage occupational mobility and market-driven reallocation rather than immediate government intervention (example: shifting factory workers into agriculture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rural settlements and education to attract youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of isolated homesteads, dedicate a central 'common' holding the school, the church, the park, and be surrounded by dwellings; education in such a community embracing study of natural objects, applied science, and handicrafts might convert youth into interested and occupied producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check urban drift, make farm-life socially and intellectually attractive by providing communal amenities and vocationally relevant education combining natural science and handicrafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target occupational-shift policy to demographics likely to adapt
rubrics_metrics.description: The old mill-hands ought not to attempt the change; but the young and middle-aged ought, and escape from their 'bondage' in the East to the free fields of the West.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When promoting large occupational shifts (e.g., to agriculture), prioritize younger and middle-aged workers who can more readily adapt and benefit, rather than older workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize structural, demographic causes of labor-market stress
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction of extravagant salaries is commendable but will not materially raise wages; native youth drawn to cities and immigrant crowds have swollen population centers and increased applicants, lowering the price of labor. Labor-saving machinery and large industries have sometimes outrun demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing wage and employment problems, account for demographic shifts, urbanization, immigration, and technological change — remedies must address structural drivers, not only managerial practices.
